extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers of The Popular Science Monthly; scientifically literate public, reviewers, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the evaluative standards and criteria used in magazine editorials and book reviews (scientific, policy, and travel/missionary books) from a late-19th-century Popular Science Monthly issue. Focuses on what the reviewer or editorial voice treats as evidence of quality, rigor, legitimacy, or proper policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific legitimacy of studying suicide
rubrics_metrics.description: Science's office is to investigate the regularities and conditions (laws) of phenomena; voluntary destruction of life is a social phenomenon amenable to scientific inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer argues that suicide falls within the scope of science just as combustion or plant-growth do; treating suicide statistically and as a set of regular phenomena is legitimate and necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic and comprehensive inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality treatment is 'systematic and comprehensive' — covering phenomena, conditions, and laws of the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Morselli's work is praised for being revised/abridged into a form that supplies a long-recognized want in literature; thorough structure and coverage are markers of authoritativeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extensive statistics and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical claims should be supported by extensive tables and numerical records of facts; statistics (numbers, averages) are central evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes 'extensive tables are given' which confirm general results; the statistician's task is described as expressing relations between suicide rates and conditions via numbers and averages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictability and regularity (seasonal/monthly variation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good analysis demonstrates predictable regularities such as monthly/seasonal variation (e.g., maximum suicides in hot season, minimum in cold).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer points to diagrams (Fig. 1) that show comparative monthly curves across countries; the ability to predict monthly variation is presented as strong evidence of scientific lawfulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disentangling multiple causal conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An investigator must disentangle many interacting causes to determine the proper value of each condition affecting the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer emphasizes complexity (many causes acting together) and lauds the work for attempting to separate and quantify individual influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of multiple influence categories
rubrics_metrics.description: A rigorous study considers physical environment, ethnological (racial) factors, social environment (civilization, religion, economy), and individual conditions (sex, age, vocation, civil status).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer lists these chapters/sections as essential content; examples are given (race differences, seasonal effects, age curves, civil status influences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear graphical presentation (figures/curves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Present data with clear figures and curves (e.g., monthly curves, age-distribution curves, civil-status influence charts) to illustrate results visually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer references Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 3 as important for conveying monthly variation, age distribution, and civil-status effects; graphical display strengthens an author's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical significance and policy relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: A valuable scientific/social study should show practical exemplification and implications — e.g., how knowledge can help diminish the practice or inform policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praises chapters on philosophy, moral aspects, and modes/instruments of self-destruction as instructive for policy and prevention; applicability is a mark of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Familiarity with local language and culture for foreign studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Study of foreign peoples is stronger when the author has familiarity with the native language and culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wheeler's experience preaching in Chinese and working with written/spoken language is cited as giving him advantages in studying character of the Chinese and producing a readable, fairer account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candor and fairness in evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when the author has a declared bias (e.g., missionary intent), candor and fairness in presenting observations are marks of quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer notes 'more candor and fairness than might be expected' from a religious partisan; balanced tone and acknowledgment of complexities are valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of missionary success: measurable vs qualitative
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicting standards for judging missionary success: (a) conventional measurable standards (numbers of converts, tangible results) and (b) qualitative/spiritual standards (one convert as triumph, moral/spiritual dynamics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer criticizes Wheeler's very liberal/peculiar standard ('Were there not a single convert... it would still be too early to pronounce unfavorably') and urges judging missions by the same practical tests used for diplomatic, commercial, and military efforts when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve canal neutrality via strong arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Panama Canal's neutrality is of first importance to world commerce; it must be preserved inviolate by strong arrangements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because Colombia is weak, treaty stipulations guaranteeing neutrality or securing equal benefits for all nations are necessary; vague or weak guarantees are inadequate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multilateral treaty guarantees to unilateral/exclusive control
rubrics_metrics.description: A valid guarantee of canal neutrality is best secured by treaty compact among all powers that could threaten it; unilateral or exclusive control by one power is inadequate and suspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer argues that the US giving itself a 'proper' guarantee or taking exclusive possession invites distrust and the possibility of violating neutrality when convenient; the stronger and more comprehensive the guarantee the better.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect existing treaties and historic policy; avoid inversion
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation's new diplomatic policy should not invert or abrogate long-established treaties and historic policy without clear justification; sudden departures call the new policy into question.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer invokes past US resolutions and treaties (including 1835/1839 congressional actions and an earlier treaty with England) that contemplated international guarantees; advocates caution against claiming the change is 'nothing more than adherence to principles long enunciated' when facts contradict that.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private enterprise efficacy for public works
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful infrastructure development often requires vigor of private enterprise and capital; legislation alone without private initiative may fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Virginia's James River & Kanawha canal project failed despite state efforts and millions spent; Northern private capital reorganized the work into a successful Richmond and Alleghany Railroad using business enterprise and modern construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial viability and adopting modern technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Public works should be evaluated for practical viability in light of current technology (e.g., railroads versus obsolete canals) and commercial utility rather than romantic or militant notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praises the railroad's rapid construction with modern improvements as of 'far greater moment' than war displays; Congress wisely declined to assume obsolete canal work when railroads were developing.
